def build_E2(layers=(10,11,12), thr=0.3, frac=1.0):
    info={}
    for l in layers:
        name=f'model.layers.{l}.mlp.up_proj.weight'
        W = load_original(name).numpy().copy()
        U,S,Vt = np.linalg.svd(W, full_matrices=False)
        d = Vt[0]
        pj = W@d
        sel = np.where(np.abs(pj)>thr)[0]
        W[sel] -= frac*np.outer(pj[sel], d)
        save_edit(name, torch.tensor(W))
        info[l]=sel.tolist()
    return info

So about 90 neurons across layers 10 to 12 all read one shared direction through their up-projections, which is very unlikely to happen naturally. However, averaged over answer tokens they are not unusually active (0.016 against a typical 0.014). At the last prompt token, v0 is present to a similar degree in math and non-math prompts. So if they matter, they probably fire on specific tokens rather than uniformly. Before testing them causally, I want to see two things. First, which tokens drive the v0 projection: I will list the highest-projecting token positions in the pass-2 prompts and summarise how v0 aligns with digit and non-digit embedding rows. Second, I will run a systematic scan of every layer and matrix for the same "many rows share one direction" signature. That will show whether layers 10 to 12 are the whole planted structure or part of something larger.

The tokens with the highest v0 projection are ordinary words such as "seeds", "wheel", "beans" and "her", and also the "model" template token. The distribution is broad (median 0.09, 99th percentile 0.45). So v0 is not an obvious digit or math-token detector, and what it does is still unclear. Before going further into these neurons, I will scan every layer and matrix type for the same signature: units whose weight vectors share one direction, measured as the share of the top singular vector carried by its top 20 units. I will compute this per row for gate/up/q/k/v and per column for down/o. The scan will show whether layers 10 to 12 are the only coordinated group or part of a larger planted circuit, for example a matching group in attention or down_proj.

The full scan confirms that layers 10, 11 and 12 up_proj are the strongest coordinated groups in the model, with 34, 38 and 39 rows at |cos| > 0.4 to the shared direction. Other MLP layers have at most about 20, except layer 25 with 99. The attention-matrix numbers are high everywhere, so they reflect natural low-dimensional structure rather than an anomaly. To decide how to undo the group, I need to know whether the planted neurons are new, dedicated units or natural neurons with a v0 component added to their up rows (row ← row + c·v0). In the first case they would be zeroed; in the second, v0 would be projected out of those rows. I will look at the distribution of the up-row projections on v0 in each of the three layers. A clearly separated cluster with one sign and a consistent size would indicate an added component, and its size relative to the rest of the row would show how much of each neuron is natural.

The projections settle it. In every layer, 99% of up rows have |projection on v0| below about 0.12, but about 30 to 40 rows sit at ±0.8 to ±1.4, with both signs. Their remaining (orthogonal) part has an ordinary norm, about 0.76 to 1.05 against a median near 1. This looks like natural neurons with a large ±c·v0 component added to their up rows. So the most surgical undo is to remove that component from those rows rather than delete the neurons. I will build edit E2: in layers 10, 11 and 12, for rows with |proj| > 0.3, subtract the projection on that layer's own top singular direction, setting the component to zero. I will then test it with a paired generation pass on DEV[:256]. If these rows carry the suppression, accuracy should rise clearly, beyond the roughly 3-point standard error. If accuracy does not move, the group is either natural or not the cause, and I will try full ablation next.
